text:
The apartment on West Seventeenth Street had the particular, museum-like hush of rooms curated by people who have entirely given up on the suburbs. My mother lived in Larchmont in a house with three types of beige carpeting. My father lived in Chelsea with a terrier named Greta Garbo, a glass table supported by two plaster greyhounds, and a rotating cast of men who called me "darling" with a theatrical sincerity that both terrified and thrilled me.

I was thirteen, an age at which one’s body feels like a poorly packed suitcase. In Larchmont, I was tall, frizzy-haired, and fundamentally invisible. In Chelsea, on every second weekend, I was treated like a visiting archduchess.

"Look at this posture," my father’s friend Arthur would say, taking my chin between fingers that smelled of lime peel and tobacco. "Richard, why are we allowing her to slouch like a wet cellist?"

"Leave her be, Arthur," my father would say from the kitchen, where he was inevitably arranging things—capers on smoked salmon, or seventeen different capsules of protease inhibitors into a sterling-silver pillbox from Tiffany’s. "She’s in her formative gloom. It’s very Russian."

It was the late nineties, that strange parenthesis when the plague had begun, for some, to recede from an immediate death sentence into a grueling management of life, though for my father the reprieve had arrived too late. His virus was what his doctor called "stubbornly vintage." He had lost the fat in his cheeks, giving him the gaunt handsomeness of an El Greco saint, and he walked with a nautical roll because neuropathy had taken the sensation from the soles of his feet.

When he announced in February that we were going on a cruise to the Mexican Riviera for spring break, my mother called him three times in forty minutes. I listened from the upstairs extension, twisting the telephone cord around my wrist.

"Richard, it’s a chartered boat," she said, using the tight-throated tone she reserved for cancer, bankruptcy, or my father’s personal life. "Do you really think that’s an appropriate environment for Clara? Six hundred men on a ship?"

"Eight hundred, actually, Deborah," my father’s voice came back, dry like tissue paper. "And unless you’re worried she’s going to pick up an aggressively well-informed opinion on Stephen Sondheim’s middle period, I think she’ll survive."

"You know what I mean," my mother said. "And your T-cells—"

"My T-cells are going to Puerto Vallarta," he said. "Let the girl pack a swimsuit. Not the navy one from Lands' End, please. It makes her look like a nineteenth-century lifeguard."

***

The ship was called the *Mayan Princess*, which my father remarked was an absurd name for a vessel registered in Panama, built in Finland, and currently occupied by the entire demographic of Fire Island Pines circa 1994.

From the moment we crossed the gangway in San Diego, it was clear my presence was a statistical anomaly. There were eight hundred and forty passengers on the manifest. Eight hundred and thirty-seven were gay men; the remaining three were a lesbian couple who served as the cruise’s legal counsel, and me.

I stood in the atrium, clutching my Jansport backpack, wearing denim overalls my father had politely asked me to leave in New York. Around us, the air was thick with the scent of Acqua di Gio, coconut tanning oil, and the manic buoyancy of men who were used to monitoring their posture on the street suddenly realizing they owned the entire floating town. Above us, a loudspeaker played a thunderous house remix of Whitney Houston.

"Well," my father said, leaning heavily on his silver-topped cane. "It’s like a circuit party at the assisted-living facility. Come along, Clara. We’re on the Promenade Deck, which means people will be jogging past our porthole at six in the morning in very small garments."

Our stateroom smelled of lemon cleanser and cold air-conditioning. While I claimed the twin bed nearest the wall, my father began the twenty-minute ritual of unpacking his pharmacy, wedging amber bottles together on the narrow bathroom shelf with rolled-up washcloths so they wouldn't rattle. Watching him, I noticed how badly his fingers trembled. His wrists had grown so thin over the winter that his gold Tank watch—a gift from a man named Julian who had died when I was nine—slid halfway down his forearm whenever he raised his glass.

"Are you going to be tired?" I asked. It was our coded question. I never asked if he was dying, and he never told me he was, though the evidence was laid out between us like silverware at every meal.

He swallowed four chalky blue ovals and looked at me in the mirror. His eyes were bright, slightly yellowed, and fiercely amused.

"I have been tired since the Carter Administration, darling," he said. "If I sleep through Mazatlán, you have my permission to tip me over the rail. Now put on some sunscreen. We have to go up to the Lido Deck and watch the homosexuals wave handkerchiefs at the Navy base."

If I had feared being treated as an intruder, I had underestimated the latent paternal instincts of eight hundred men on vacation. By the second day, I had become the ship’s unofficial mascot. Because I was with Richard—and everyone seemed to know Richard from New York, or at least recognize the noble geometry of his wasted cheekbones—I was folded into the collective embrace. In Larchmont, thirteen-year-old girls were scrutinized for their flaws; on the *Mayan Princess*, I was treated as a concept, and the concept was fabulous.

At breakfast, a massive man from Atlanta named Bear—with a graying beard and shoulders like Virginia hams shoved into a floral shirt—would intercept my tray. "Sweetheart, don't touch the scrambled eggs out of the trough," he’d rumble, steering me toward the omelette station. "They’re powdered. Make the nice boy do you egg whites with feta and spinach. You need protein if you're gonna survive the tea dance."

By the pool, while my father dozed under a yellow umbrella wrapped in two terrycloth robes despite the eighty-degree heat, a trio of flight attendants from Chicago taught me spades and explained the social strata of the ship.

"See those boys by the jacuzzi?" said Gregory, gesturing with his daiquiri toward five men whose abdominal muscles looked vacuum-sealed. "Los Angeles muscle queens. They haven't eaten a carbohydrate since the Northridge earthquake. Very decorative, zero conversation. Over by the shuffleboard? Boston money. They’ll buy you a Shirley Temple and tell you about their historic preservation project in Provincetown until your ears bleed."

"What about you guys?" I asked, dealing the damp cards onto my towel.

"Us?" Gregory adjusted his sunglasses. "We’re the Midwest chorus line, honey. Low maintenance, high alcohol tolerance, deep emotional availability."

For the first time in my life, I didn't feel awkward. My frizzy hair was declared "very Pre-Raphaelite" by a hairdresser from Toronto who braided it with silk ribbon salvaged from a duty-free box. My sarcasm, which usually got me sent to the guidance counselor at home, was greeted at our dinner table with wild applause.

"She’s got your timing, Richard," said our tablemate, an architect named Simon whose own partner had died the previous autumn. "God help the straight boys in Westchester when she figures out how to use it for evil."

My father would just smile, hiding minuscule pieces of prime rib under his parsley so the waiter wouldn't fuss. At night, as the ship pitched through the dark Pacific, I would hear him get up three or four times, the slow *thump-scrape* of his cane against the carpet, followed by the running tap. I would lie in the dark, trying to memorize the exact cadence of his breathing so I would still have it when I went back to New York.

***

On the fourth day, we anchored off Cabo San Lucas. My father woke up with a low-grade fever that left his sheets damp and smelling faintly of vinegar. The ship’s doctor listened to his lungs and suggested he stay out of the sun for twenty-four hours.

"Go up and read your book," my father told me, propped against three pillows, looking remarkably small in his striped pajamas. "Don't sit in here watching me expire like Little Eva. It’s terrible for my vanity."

"I can read to you," I said.

"You are reading *Jane Eyre*," he said, closing his eyes. "If I have to listen to one more chapter about typhus at the Lowood School, I really shall pass on. Go get an ice cream. Tell Gregory to make sure you don't get sunburned."

I didn't go to the Lido Deck. Without my father in his chair, the wall-to-wall joy of the pool area felt too loud. Instead, I climbed to the deserted Sports Deck, wandering toward the aft rail where the giant blue funnel hummed like a refrigerator. Sitting on a coil of rope in the shade of a lifeboat, wearing an oversized gray crew polo, was a boy.

He was maybe fifteen, with dark hair and skin the color of a toasted almond, half-heartedly scraping rust off a brass stanchion with steel wool. When he saw me, he stopped, squinting.

"You're the girl," he said, his English carrying a soft, rhythmic tilt.

"I'm Clara," I said, leaning my elbows on the hot teak rail.

"I'm Mateo," he said, tossing the steel wool into a bucket. "My uncle is the chief steward. Since school is out in Ensenada, my mother made him take me on so I don't hang out by the beach and get in trouble." He looked around the deck, where a massive rainbow flag snapped from the stern flagpole. "This boat is crazy, man."

I stiffened, my middle-school defenses rising. "What's wrong with it?"

Mateo laughed and offered me a warm piece of cinnamon gum from his pocket. "Nothing's wrong with it. It’s the best charter of the year. My uncle says on the straight cruises, guys get drunk on Coors Light, throw up in the plants, and leave two dollars on the dresser. Here? Yesterday a guy in a pink sarong gave me twenty bucks just for bringing him extra limes. Plus, nobody looks at the waitresses like creeps."

I unwrapped the gum, the tension leaving my shoulders. "Yeah. They're really nice."

"You here with your dad?"

"Yeah."

Mateo nodded toward the jagged brown rocks of Land's End. "I saw him at dinner. The tall guy with the stick. He looks like my grandfather before his liver went bad." He said it without pity, with flat, unvarnished pragmatism. "He sick?"

"Yeah," I said. In Larchmont, my mother had instructed me to say he had "an autoimmune condition similar to lupus," a lie that felt like chewing on aluminum foil. "He has AIDS."

Mateo nodded again, blowing a small pink bubble. "My cousin Hector in San Diego had that. He died two years ago. Your dad looks pretty cool, though. He was wearing a purple jacket at the captain’s dinner."

"It’s vintage Halston," I said automatically. "He got it in Milan in 1978."

Mateo grinned, showing a slightly crooked canine that made my stomach do a strange, slow flip. "See? Cool. Come on, I'll show you where we keep the ice cream machine that isn't locked up after lunch."

For the next two hours, while the passengers were ashore in Cabo, Mateo took me through the steel arteries of the crew quarters out onto the narrow bow deck reserved for the boatswain’s mates. We sat on the anchor chain housing with paper bowls of melting chocolate soft-serve. He told me about his band in Ensenada, and I told him how I hated Larchmont. He didn't ask why I was so tall, or what it was like to have a gay father. When the wind blew a braided strand of my hair across my face, he reached over and untangled it from the ribbon, his fingers smelling of brass polish and chocolate. His knuckles grazed my cheekbone, and we both stopped talking for a second, looking down at the clear green water thirty feet below.

"You coming to the big party tomorrow night?" he asked, resting his hand back on his knee. "The crew goes up on the bridge roof to watch because everybody dresses up."

"I think so," I said. "If my dad feels okay."

"I'll look for you," Mateo said.

***

The party on the fifth night, as we steamed toward Puerto Vallarta, was officially titled the "White Party."

"The premise," my father explained before our stateroom mirror while I helped fasten his cufflinks, "is that everyone wears white to symbolize purity, unity, and the fact that they haven't touched fried chicken since April. In reality, after midnight, someone inevitably spills cranberry vodka down their front and cries in the stairwell over an ex-boyfriend from Seattle. Hand me that silk scarf, darling. My neck looks like a plucked turkey."

He had rallied since Cabo through sheer stubbornness and a double dose of prednisone. His ivory linen suit hung from his shoulders like clothes on a wire hanger, though with the white silk scarf tucked into the collar, he still looked dashing—like a disgraced British diplomat in a Graham Greene novel. I wore a white cotton sundress that Gregory and Simon had bought for me in the ship’s boutique after staging a polite intervention regarding my overalls. Standing next to my father in the narrow mirror, with my hair unbraided and brushed out over my shoulders, I didn't look like a girl from Larchmont anymore. I looked like Richard’s daughter.

The Lido Deck had been transformed. Massive white parachutes rigged between the lifeboat davits billowed in the ocean wind, glowing violet and blue under stage lights. The pool was covered by a wooden dance floor, and at the center of it, six hundred men in white jeans, linen tunics, and angel wings moved in a single, undulating wave beneath a shower of artificial soap-flake snow. The house music was so loud I could feel the bass in my teeth, a woman’s voice singing over and over: *Hold on now, hold on now.*

When we stepped out, a cheer went up from our dinner table’s contingent. Bear lifted me off the deck in a hug smelling of coconut rum, while Simon pressed a ginger ale into my hand and pulled out a cushioned teak chair for my father.

"Richard, you bastard," Simon shouted over the music, kissing his cheeks. "You’re outdressing the entire boat."

"It’s the lighting, Simon," my father called back, settling carefully into the chair and resting both hands on his cane. "Under blacklight, jaundice reads as a St. Tropez tan."

I looked up toward the dark wing of the bridge, two decks above. Silhouetted against the stars, three figures in gray crew shirts leaned over the rail. One of them raised a hand in a quick, two-fingered wave. I waved back, a small, secret electricity humming beneath my ribs.

On the dance floor, the atmosphere was shifting into something almost liturgical. I was thirteen, and I didn't yet know the full history of the rooms these men had danced in over the last fifteen years, or how many ghosts were crowded onto that wooden platform. What I did know, watching Gregory throw his head back under the soap-flake snow, watching Bear wrap his enormous arms around three smaller men at once as the chorus peaked, was that nobody here was taking the air in their lungs for granted. There was a ferocity to their joy that made the polite dinner parties in Westchester look like rehearsals for being dead. They were holding each other up, and the music was keeping the dark water outside the rails from coming in.

Around eleven o'clock, the DJ blended the pounding beat down, letting it fade into the vinyl crackle of a slow record, and the opening strings of a lush orchestration of "The Way We Were" drifted over the ocean. Half the men groaned campily; the other half immediately pulled their partners close.

Beside me, I heard the rasp of wood against teak. My father had stood up.

He left his cane hooked over the chair arm, getting his balance against the slow roll of the Pacific swell, buttoning his jacket with a trembling hand. Then he turned to me and held out his arm, bowing slightly.

"May I have this dance, Miss Bennett?" he asked.

"Are your feet okay?" I asked, my voice catching.

"My feet are entirely ornamental at this juncture," he said. "Which means you won't have to worry about stepping on them."

We walked onto the edge of the floor. The sea of men in white parted for us with a quiet, immediate choreography, forming a warm, breathing wall of linen and cotton that sheltered us from the wind. My father put his right hand on my shoulder blade and took my hand in his left. When I stepped in close, my forehead rested just below his collarbone. He felt like a bird inside the linen suit—all hollow bones and fierce, rapid heartbeat. I held him with the same careful lightness I used when picking up the glass greyhounds on his coffee table.

We mostly swayed in place as the ship lifted and fell beneath us, purple lights sweeping across our shoulders.

"You've had a good time?" he murmured into my hair, his breath rattling slightly at the bottom of his lungs.

"The best," I said into his lapel, which smelled of lavender water and the dry heat of his fever.

"Good," he said, his thumb moving across my knuckles. "I wanted you to see it. Not the boat—the boat is ridiculous. Just... how people take care of one another when they aren't related by blood. You're going to be fine, Clara. You know how to find your people."

"You're my people," I said, and for the first time all week, I started to cry, my tears leaving dark spots on his white silk scarf.

"Well, yes," he said softly, resting his sharp chin on my head, letting his weight settle onto me just a fraction before straightening up again. "Obviously. I have custody on alternate weekends."

Around us, the music swelled into its final crescendo. Through the blur of my eyelashes, I saw Gregory wiping his face with a cocktail napkin; I saw Simon looking out over the dark water toward Mexico, his hand resting on Bear’s massive shoulder; I looked up toward the bridge and saw Mateo still leaning against the rail, watching us as the soap-flake snow drifted down through the floodlights and melted into our hair. We stayed out there until the record spun down into the quiet hiss of the speakers, and the engines of the *Mayan Princess* were the only sound left in the night, pushing us steadily south through the warm, dark water toward the morning.
